title: "Job Scheduling"
description: "The process of assigning computational jobs to resources and deciding when they should run."
term: "Job Scheduling"
letter: "J"

difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

Job scheduling decides which computational task should run, when it should
start, and which machine or accelerator should run it. It helps teams share
limited resources such as GPUs and cluster nodes.

## Technical explanation

A scheduler manages jobs with requirements and constraints, such as CPU or GPU
capacity, memory, priority, dependencies, deadlines, and retry policies. It
places jobs onto available resources while trying to meet goals such as
throughput, fairness, and utilization.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Training and evaluation jobs can consume large amounts of accelerator time.
Effective scheduling reduces idle resources, coordinates concurrent
experiments, and makes long-running workloads more reliable and predictable.

## How it works

A job is submitted with its resource requests and execution instructions. The
scheduler checks those requirements against available capacity, queues the job
if resources are unavailable, and assigns it when suitable resources become
available. It can also monitor execution, retry failures, and release resources
when the job completes.

## Practical example

A team submits several model-training runs that each require one GPU. A cluster
scheduler queues runs until GPUs are free, starts them on eligible machines,
and records their completion status for the experiment-tracking system.

## Common misconceptions

- Scheduling is not the same as orchestration: orchestration coordinates
  broader workflows, while a scheduler makes placement and timing decisions.
- A job waiting in a queue is not necessarily stuck; requested resources or
  scheduling constraints may not currently be satisfied.
- High utilization alone does not guarantee fairness or short job wait times.
